Selling a used phone in Europe

Phones are the most common second-hand electronics, and the easiest to get wrong. A locked phone or the wrong storage size can turn a good deal into a loss.

Updated 2026-10-12 · by FlipLens

What drives the price

  • Exact model: standard, Plus, Pro and Max versions differ a lot in value.
  • Storage: more storage sells for more. Check it in the settings, not just on the box.
  • Battery health: many phones show the battery condition in the settings; a weak battery lowers the price.
  • Condition: screen scratches or cracks, back glass, frame dents, camera lenses, buttons and ports.
  • Completeness: box and cable help a little; the phone itself matters most.

Account locks and carrier locks

A phone that is still linked to the previous owner's account (for example Apple's Activation Lock or a Google account after a reset) cannot be set up by a new owner and is worth only a fraction of the price. Make sure the seller removes the account and resets the phone in front of you. Also check whether the phone is locked to a mobile network: unlocked phones sell to more buyers.

Common mistakes

  • Buying a phone that is still signed in to an account.
  • Comparing prices of a different storage size or version.
  • Not checking for a replaced or non-original screen.
  • Ignoring battery health.

Quick checklist

  • Model and storage confirmed in the settings.
  • Signed out of all accounts and factory reset.
  • Not locked to a network.
  • Battery health checked.
  • Screen, cameras, speakers, microphone and charging port tested.

Questions

What should I check before buying a used phone?

That it is signed out of all accounts and reset, not locked to a network, has the storage you expect, a healthy battery, and a working screen, cameras and charging port.

Does storage size change the resale value?

Yes. The same model with more storage usually sells for more, so always compare the same storage size.
